candidates.sector_or_industry: AI accelerators, GPU systems, networking and AI infrastructure platforms
candidates.theme_relation: NVIDIA is the central accelerator and rack-scale compute supplier for the current AI infrastructure cycle; its data-center compute availability gates many downstream cloud, neocloud and enterprise AI deployments.

candidates.theme_relation: Broadcom maps directly to hyperscaler custom AI accelerator demand and AI networking, making it a high-priority candidate for the non-GPU accelerator and network-scaling nodes.

candidates.theme_relation: SK hynix is a leading HBM and server-memory supplier; HBM is a high-priority AI chokepoint because accelerator capacity is constrained by memory qualification, packaging coordination, yield and customer allocation.

candidates.sector_or_industry: AI-native cloud infrastructure
candidates.theme_relation: CoreWeave is a concentrated public pure-play for AI compute capacity monetization, converting GPU and data-center capacity into contracted AI cloud revenue.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Hyperscale cloud, AI infrastructure, enterprise software and AI applications
source_nodes: Hyperscaler AI capex and cloud demand
candidates.theme_relation: Microsoft is both a demand-side hyperscaler driving AI infrastructure capex and a monetization platform through Azure AI, Copilot and enterprise AI services.

candidates.sector_or_industry: AWS cloud infrastructure, AI chips, hyperscale data centers and e-commerce platform AI
source_nodes: Hyperscaler AI capex and cloud demand
candidates.theme_relation: Amazon is a major AI infrastructure buyer/operator through AWS and a demand driver for GPUs, internal AI chips, servers, networking, power and data-center capacity.

candidates.sector_or_industry: AI infrastructure, social platforms, recommendation systems, generative AI and advertising technology
source_nodes: Hyperscaler AI capex and cloud demand
candidates.theme_relation: Meta is a large AI infrastructure capex driver; its AI data-center buildout creates pull-through for accelerators, memory, networking, power, cooling and construction capacity.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Cloud infrastructure and enterprise software
candidates.theme_relation: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is positioned as an AI training and inference capacity provider; its AI relevance depends on converting signed AI demand into GPU supply, data-center capacity and profitable cloud revenue.

candidates.sector_or_industry: AI servers, enterprise infrastructure and systems integration
candidates.theme_relation: Dell is a practical deployment-layer candidate because GPU supply and AI demand become monetizable only after servers and rack-scale systems are integrated, delivered, powered and accepted.

candidates.theme_relation: Wesco is a second-order AI capex beneficiary with unusually direct data-center sales disclosure; it can benefit if electrical, cabling, communications and logistics timing become constraints for AI data-center commissioning.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Electrical connection, enclosures, liquid cooling and data-center power components
candidates.theme_relation: nVent maps to the thermal and electrical complexity of high-density AI racks, including liquid cooling and power distribution infrastructure for NVIDIA-class AI data-center systems.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Thermal management and data-center cooling systems
candidates.theme_relation: Modine is tied to AI data-center buildouts through engineered cooling capacity; high-density AI racks raise the importance of air and liquid thermal-management systems.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Mechanical and electrical building services / specialty contractor
candidates.theme_relation: Comfort Systems maps to the physical-capacity conversion layer: AI data-center demand requires electrical, mechanical, modular construction and building-systems execution before GPU clusters can generate revenue.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Data-center REIT and colocation/hyperscale infrastructure
candidates.theme_relation: Digital Realty is an AI infrastructure enabler where physical data-center capacity, power access and pre-leased hyperscale deployments determine how quickly AI demand becomes operational capacity.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Industrial machinery and power-generation equipment
candidates.theme_relation: Caterpillar is an underappreciated AI infrastructure candidate if grid interconnection, reliability or time-to-power constraints increase demand for large engines, turbines and generator sets for data-center applications.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Mechanical/electrical construction, industrial and energy infrastructure services
candidates.theme_relation: EMCOR maps to the buildout layer that gates AI data-center monetization through electrical, mechanical and infrastructure services, although the exact AI/data-center share of backlog requires validation.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Data-center colocation, interconnection and digital infrastructure
candidates.theme_relation: Equinix captures AI demand through colocation, cloud-adjacent networking and interconnection, though its AI exposure is broader and less pure-play than neocloud or hyperscale shell-capacity providers.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Commercial HVAC, thermal management and liquid cooling
candidates.theme_relation: Trane maps to the AI cooling bottleneck through central plant, heat rejection, controls and LiquidStack direct-to-chip and immersion-cooling capabilities.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Enterprise software, CRM, data platform and agentic AI applications
candidates.theme_relation: Salesforce is relevant to the software monetization layer because Agentforce and Data 360 ARR provide a measurable way to track enterprise AI adoption beyond product announcements.

candidates.sector_or_industry: Enterprise workflow automation, IT operations and agentic AI software
candidates.theme_relation: ServiceNow is a candidate for the enterprise AI workflow layer where value should be validated through paid automation use cases, AI specialists, workflow adoption and renewal or expansion evidence.

coverage_gaps: The merged universe is still US-heavy and underrepresents Taiwan, Korea, Japan and Europe suppliers in foundry, CoWoS/advanced packaging, substrates, passive components, optics, semiconductor equipment, memory equipment and electrical infrastructure.

HBM is represented by SK hynix, but a full Layer 1C universe should add and validate Samsung Electronics, Micron, TSMC, ASE, Amkor, substrate suppliers and HBM-related equipment/materials companies where public-market access and evidence quality allow.

Optical networking and CPO exposure is underrepresented; later layers should validate credible public names in Ethernet switching, optical modules, DSPs, lasers, EMLs, silicon photonics, connectors and test equipment.

Power/grid exposure is only partially covered through Caterpillar, Wesco, nVent and construction contractors; later layers need transformer, switchgear, UPS, grid interconnection, gas turbine, power EPC and utility names with AI-specific revenue or backlog evidence.

The software layer currently includes Salesforce and ServiceNow but lacks a broader enterprise AI monetization universe across security, data infrastructure, observability, developer tools, databases and model platforms.
The universe does not yet include market-pricing, valuation, margin quality, customer concentration, balance-sheet risk or estimate-revision checks; those belong in later Serenity layers.

memory_update.text: AI should be tracked as a multi-layer capital cycle rather than a single semiconductor theme: demand begins with hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprise automation, then pulls on accelerators, HBM, custom silicon, networking, servers, data-center shells, cooling, electrical systems, power generation and grid interconnection.

Highest-priority Layer 2 validation paths are accelerators/custom silicon, HBM and advanced packaging, AI cloud capacity conversion, data-center power/cooling, electrical distribution, construction execution and enterprise AI ARR monetization.

Power, cooling and construction should remain high-priority AI chokepoint candidates because AI data centers can exceed 100 MW and monetization can be delayed even when model demand and GPU orders are strong.

Layer 1C universe is not yet globally complete; next expansion should add Taiwan/Korea/Japan/EU names across foundry, HBM, substrates, advanced packaging, optics, equipment, power equipment and grid infrastructure.

Later funnel steps must separate AI-specific revenue and backlog from generic data-center or cloud exposure, then add valuation, market-pricing, margin quality, customer concentration and falsification checks.

summary: Merged Layer 1 universe for the AI theme from cached Layer 1A theme map and visible Layer 1B node-level candidate outputs. The universe is intentionally broad across AI demand, cloud/neocloud capacity, accelerators, custom silicon, HBM/memory, AI servers, data-center REITs, liquid cooling, electrical distribution, construction execution, power generation, and enterprise AI monetization. Ranking reflects preliminary Serenity relevance before deeper validation: higher scores go to companies closer to measurable demand, physical or technical chokepoints, explicit AI revenue/backlog/capex evidence, or scarce deployment capacity. This is research support only and does not provide buy/sell recommendations, target prices, or expected returns.
